problem: Consider the equation ${y}^{″}-6{y}^{′}+10y=0$ where $y=y(t).$ If $y={e}^{\lambda t}$ is a solution, then $\lambda =$
worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda t}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda t},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda t}-6\lambda {e}^{\lambda t}+10{e}^{\lambda t} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda t}({\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +10) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +10=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +10 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +9)-9+10 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)^{2}+1 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)^{2} & =-1 \\ \lambda -3 & =\pm \text{i} \\ \lambda  & =3\pm \text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  $\lambda =3\pm \text{i}$ are the complex roots of the auxiliary equation.
